ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a titration curve of pH changing with the volume of NaOH added; the horizontal axis is labeled Volume NaOH (mL), and the vertical axis is pH. The curve shows two obvious equivalence-point jumps: one smaller jump near about 10 mL, and another very steep jump near about 20 mL. Reasoning: The stem states that the diprotic acid H2C2O4 is titrated with the strong base NaOH. A diprotic acid has two acidic protons that can be neutralized, so the two equivalence points correspond to the first and second neutralization steps, respectively. In the figure, 20 mL is at the second equivalence point; at this time, both acidic protons have been neutralized by NaOH, and the main oxalate-containing species from the acid source should be the fully deprotonated conjugate base C2O4^2−, not H2C2O4 or HC2O4^−.

method.method_draft: First describe the graph: it is a pH versus volume of NaOH titration curve with two equivalence jumps, around 10 mL and 20 mL. Use the text to identify the acid as diprotic H2C2O4 and the titrant as strong base NaOH. Since 20 mL is the second equivalence point, both acidic protons have been neutralized, so the dominant oxalate-containing species is the fully deprotonated conjugate base, C2O4^2−.

method.method_draft: From the plotted titration curve, identify the equivalence volumes as approximately 10 mL and 20 mL. Combine this with the text value 0.10 M NaOH: 10 mL corresponds to 0.0010 mol OH−, the amount needed to remove the first proton from all acid molecules, while 20 mL corresponds to 0.0020 mol OH−, enough to remove two protons from each original H2C2O4 molecule.
